theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Diode Circuits and Calculations

Taking the logarithm of the forward Shockley equation gives V_D = nV_T ln(I_D/I_S). Two operating points of the same diode therefore differ in voltage by nV_T times the natural log of their current ratio, and I_S cancels out. With n = 1 and V_T = 26 mV a tenfold rise in current needs only about 60 mV more, and doubling the current needs about 18 mV. This is why the forward drop of a conducting silicon diode stays close to 0.6 to 0.8 V over several decades of current, which justifies the constant-voltage model.

theoryAdd.plainText: V2 - V1 = n VT ln(I2/I1)   (about 60 mV per decade for n = 1)

theoryAdd.text: Two kinds of resistance describe a diode. The static or DC resistance R_D = V_D/I_D is the ratio at one operating point and is tens to hundreds of ohms. The dynamic (AC) resistance r_d = nV_T/I_D is the slope of the curve at that point, is only a few ohms at milliampere currents, and is the one used for small signals superimposed on a DC bias. The operating point itself is where the diode curve meets the load line I_D = (V_S − V_D)/R drawn from V_S/R on the current axis to V_S on the voltage axis.

Worked example 1: diode current and resistances
Given: 5 V source, 1 kΩ series resistor, silicon diode (0.7 V), n = 1, V_T = 26 mV
Step 1  I_D = (5 − 0.7) / 1 kΩ = 4.3 mA
Step 2  Static resistance R_D = 0.7 V / 4.3 mA ≈ 163 Ω
Step 3  Dynamic resistance r_d = 26 mV / 4.3 mA ≈ 6.0 Ω
Step 4  Raising I_D to 43 mA would raise V_D by only 26 mV × ln 10 ≈ 60 mV

theoryAdd.plainText: Vr(pp) ~ Idc / (fr C), fr = f (half-wave) or 2f (full-wave)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 2: bridge rectifier with capacitor filter
Given: 12 V rms secondary, 50 Hz, silicon bridge, load 100 mA, C = 1000 µF
Step 1  V_m = 12 × √2 = 16.97 V
Step 2  Two diodes conduct in series: V_m(out) = 16.97 − 1.4 = 15.57 V
Step 3  Without the capacitor: V_dc = 2 × 15.57 / π = 9.91 V
Step 4  Ripple frequency f_r = 2 × 50 = 100 Hz
Step 5  With the capacitor: V_r(pp) = 0.1 / (100 × 1000 µF) = 1.0 V
Step 6  V_dc ≈ 15.57 − 1.0/2 ≈ 15.1 V

A clipper removes the part of a waveform beyond a set level: a shunt diode in series with a battery V_B starts conducting when the output reaches V_B plus the diode drop, so the output is held there. A clamper uses a series capacitor and a shunt diode. On the first peak the capacitor charges to the peak voltage minus the diode drop, and afterwards it acts as a battery that shifts the whole waveform up or down without changing its peak-to-peak value. The RC time constant must be much longer than the signal period so the capacitor does not discharge between peaks.

Worked example 3: Zener regulator design and check
Given: V_in = 12 V, V_Z = 6 V, load 20 mA, desired I_Z = 10 mA
Step 1  I_R = I_Z + I_L = 10 + 20 = 30 mA
Step 2  R_S = (12 − 6) / 30 mA = 200 Ω
Step 3  Load removed: I_Z = 30 mA, P_Z = 6 V × 30 mA = 180 mW
Step 4  Choose a Zener rated well above 180 mW (e.g. 400 mW)

items: Forgetting that a bridge has two diode drops in the conducting path while a centre-tapped rectifier has one.
Using the rms value where the peak is needed: V_m = √2 × V_rms.
Assuming a Zener regulates before checking that the open-circuit voltage across it exceeds V_Z.
Mixing up PIV: 2V_m for the centre-tapped circuit, V_m for the bridge and half-wave circuits.
Using the static resistance V_D/I_D in a small-signal problem, where the dynamic resistance nV_T/I_D is required.

theoryAdd.text: When two diodes of different material are in parallel, the one with the lower knee voltage (germanium, 0.3 V) turns on first and clamps the voltage, so the silicon diode never reaches 0.7 V and carries no current.

questions.questionText: The depletion region of an unbiased pn junction consists mainly of:
options: A high concentration of free electrons and holes
Immobile ionised donor and acceptor atoms with almost no free carriers
Only free electrons that have diffused from the n side
Neutral atoms of the intrinsic semiconductor
questions.explanation: Majority carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving uncovered positive donor ions on the n side and negative acceptor ions on the p side; the region is depleted of mobile carriers.

questions.questionText: When the forward bias applied to a pn junction is increased, the width of the depletion region:
questions.explanation: Forward bias opposes the built-in potential, pushing majority carriers towards the junction and narrowing the depletion layer.

questions.questionText: For a silicon diode carrying a constant forward current, a rise in junction temperature causes its forward voltage to:
questions.explanation: Because I_S rises steeply with temperature, less voltage is needed for the same current; the forward drop has a temperature coefficient of about −2 mV/°C.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode (practical model, V_D = 0.7 V) is connected in forward bias in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 5 V DC supply. The diode current is:
questions.explanation: I = (5 − 0.7)/1 kΩ = 4.3 mA. Ignoring the drop gives 5 mA; using 0.3 V (germanium) gives 4.7 mA.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode has I_S = 1 × 10^-13 A and n = 1. Taking V_T = 26 mV, the forward current at V_D = 0.60 V is about:
For a diode with ideality factor n = 2 at V_T = 26 mV, the increase in forward voltage needed to raise the current tenfold is about:
questions.explanation: ΔV = nV_T ln(10) = 2 × 26 mV × 2.303 ≈ 120 mV. With n = 1 it would be about 60 mV.

questions.questionText: A diode (n = 1, V_T = 26 mV) has a forward drop of 0.650 V at 1 mA. Using the Shockley equation, its forward voltage at 20 mA is about:
The dynamic (AC) resistance of a forward-biased diode with n = 1 at I_D = 2 mA and V_T = 26 mV is:
questions.explanation: r_d = nV_T/I_D = 26 mV / 2 mA = 13 Ω.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode has a forward voltage of 0.65 V when it carries 5 mA. Its static (DC) resistance at this point is:
questions.explanation: R_D = V_D/I_D = 0.65 V / 5 mA = 130 Ω. The 5.2 Ω value is the dynamic resistance 26 mV/5 mA, which is a different quantity.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the dynamic resistance r_d of a forward-biased diode is correct?
options: It is equal to V_D/I_D at the operating point
It is inversely proportional to the DC current through the diode
It increases as the forward current increases
It is independent of the operating point
questions.explanation: r_d = nV_T/I_D is the slope of the V-I curve at the Q-point; doubling I_D halves r_d. V_D/I_D is the static resistance.

questions.questionText: A diode biased at I_D = 0.5 mA (n = 1, V_T = 25 mV) is fed a 10 mV peak AC signal through a 950 Ω series resistor, with the DC bias path having no effect on the AC signal. The peak AC voltage across the diode is:
questions.explanation: r_d = 25 mV / 0.5 mA = 50 Ω. By voltage division v_d = 10 mV × 50/(950 + 50) = 0.5 mV.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode (0.7 V) and a germanium diode (0.3 V) are connected in series, both forward biased, with a 2.2 kΩ resistor across a 12 V DC supply. The circuit current is:
A silicon diode is connected in reverse bias in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 10 V DC supply. Using the practical model, the voltage across the resistor is about:
questions.explanation: A reverse-biased diode behaves as an open circuit, so almost no current flows; the resistor drop is about 0 V and nearly all 10 V appears across the diode.

questions.questionText: A silicon diode (0.7 V) and a germanium diode (0.3 V) are connected in parallel, both forward biased, and fed from a 10 V DC supply through a 1 kΩ resistor. The current through the silicon diode is about:
questions.explanation: The germanium diode turns on first and holds the parallel voltage at 0.3 V, below the 0.7 V the silicon diode needs, so the silicon diode carries practically no current; the germanium diode carries (10 − 0.3)/1 k = 9.7 mA.

questions.questionText: Two identical silicon diodes (0.7 V) are connected in parallel and fed from a 5 V DC supply through a 430 Ω resistor. Assuming they share current equally, the current in each diode is:
questions.explanation: Total current = (5 − 0.7)/430 = 10 mA; shared equally, each diode carries 5.0 mA.

questions.questionText: A half-wave rectifier with an ideal diode is fed a sinusoidal voltage of 20 V peak. The average (DC) output voltage across a resistive load is:
questions.explanation: V_dc = V_m/π = 20/π = 6.37 V. The value 2V_m/π = 12.7 V applies to a full-wave rectifier.

questions.questionText: A bridge rectifier using silicon diodes (0.7 V each) is fed from a transformer secondary of 12 V rms and drives a resistive load with no filter. The average output voltage is about:
questions.explanation: V_m = 12√2 = 16.97 V; two diodes conduct, so the output peak is 16.97 − 1.4 = 15.57 V and V_dc = 2 × 15.57/π = 9.91 V.

questions.questionText: In a centre-tapped full-wave rectifier each half of the secondary delivers 15 V peak. With ideal diodes, the peak inverse voltage across each diode is:
questions.explanation: When one diode conducts, the non-conducting diode sees the full secondary: PIV = 2V_m = 2 × 15 = 30 V.

questions.questionText: For the same peak secondary voltage V_m per diode path, which rectifier requires diodes with a peak inverse voltage rating of 2V_m?
options: None; every rectifier requires only V_m
questions.explanation: In the centre-tapped circuit the reverse-biased diode sees the voltage of both halves of the secondary, 2V_m; in the bridge each diode sees only V_m.

questions.questionText: A full-wave rectifier is supplied from 50 Hz mains. The fundamental frequency of the ripple in its output is:
questions.explanation: A full-wave rectifier produces two output pulses per input cycle, so the ripple frequency is 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

questions.questionText: The ripple factor of an unfiltered full-wave rectifier with a resistive load is about:
questions.explanation: γ = √((V_rms/V_dc)² − 1) with V_rms = V_m/√2 and V_dc = 2V_m/π gives √(π²/8 − 1) ≈ 0.48; the half-wave value is 1.21.

questions.questionText: The maximum theoretical rectification efficiency (DC load power divided by AC input power) of a half-wave rectifier is:
questions.explanation: η = P_dc/P_ac = (V_m/π)²/(V_m/2)² = 4/π² = 0.405, i.e. 40.5 %; a full-wave rectifier reaches 8/π² = 81.1 %.

questions.questionText: A full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz mains feeds a 100 mA load through a 1000 µF reservoir capacitor. The approximate peak-to-peak ripple voltage is:
questions.explanation: V_r(pp) = I/(f_r C) with f_r = 2 × 50 = 100 Hz: 0.1/(100 × 1000 × 10^-6) = 1.0 V. Using 50 Hz gives the half-wave value, 2.0 V.

questions.questionText: A half-wave rectifier with a silicon diode (0.7 V) is fed a 10 V peak sine wave and drives a 1 kΩ resistive load. The average load current is about:
questions.explanation: Peak current = (10 − 0.7)/1 kΩ = 9.3 mA; average for a half-wave = I_m/π = 9.3/π = 2.96 mA.

questions.questionText: In a shunt clipper, a silicon diode (0.7 V) in series with a 3 V battery is connected across the output, arranged so that it conducts when the output exceeds the battery voltage. A 10 V peak sine wave is applied through a series resistor. The positive peak of the output is:
questions.explanation: The diode conducts once the output reaches V_B + V_D = 3 + 0.7 = 3.7 V, so the positive peaks are clipped at 3.7 V.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes a clipper from a clamper?
options: A clipper shifts the DC level, while a clamper removes part of the waveform
Both remove part of the waveform, but a clamper needs a battery
A clamper needs no capacitor, while a clipper always needs one
A clipper removes part of the waveform, while a clamper shifts the DC level without changing the waveform's shape
questions.explanation: Clippers cut off the part of the signal beyond a reference level; clampers use a capacitor and diode to add a DC shift while keeping the peak-to-peak value.

questions.questionText: A ±5 V square wave is applied to an ideal-diode positive clamper (series capacitor, shunt diode), whose RC time constant is much longer than the period. The output swings between:
questions.explanation: The capacitor charges to 5 V during the negative half and then adds 5 V to the input, shifting the ±5 V wave up to 0 V to +10 V; peak-to-peak stays 10 V.

questions.questionText: A 10 V peak sine wave is applied to a clamper: a series capacitor followed by a silicon diode (0.7 V) whose anode is connected to the output and cathode to ground, with a long RC time constant. In the steady state, the output swings between about:
questions.explanation: On positive peaks the diode conducts and the capacitor charges to 10 − 0.7 = 9.3 V, so v_out = v_in − 9.3 V, which ranges from +0.7 V to −19.3 V.

questions.questionText: For a clamper circuit to keep the output waveform shape undistorted, its RC time constant should be:
options: Much smaller than the period of the input signal
Much larger than the period of the input signal
Exactly equal to half the period
Equal to the diode's reverse recovery time
questions.explanation: A long time constant (typically RC ≥ 5T or more) keeps the capacitor from discharging noticeably between peaks, so the shift stays constant.

questions.questionText: A two-level clipper has two silicon diodes (0.7 V) across the output: one in series with a +4 V battery that limits positive swings, and one in series with a 6 V battery that limits negative swings. A 10 V peak sine wave is applied through a series resistor. The output is limited to between about:
questions.explanation: Each branch conducts when the output exceeds its battery voltage plus 0.7 V: the positive peaks are clipped at 4 + 0.7 = 4.7 V and the negative peaks at −(6 + 0.7) = −6.7 V.

questions.questionText: Zener breakdown, as distinct from avalanche breakdown, is characterised by:
options: Lightly doped junctions, a breakdown voltage above about 6 V and a positive temperature coefficient
Carrier multiplication by impact ionisation in a wide depletion layer
Heavily doped junctions, a breakdown voltage below about 5 V and a negative temperature coefficient
questions.explanation: In heavily doped junctions the thin depletion layer lets the strong field pull electrons directly out of bonds (field emission) at low voltage; this breakdown voltage falls as temperature rises. Avalanche breakdown occurs in lightly doped junctions at higher voltage.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the temperature coefficient of Zener diodes is correct?
options: Diodes rated near 5 to 6 V have a temperature coefficient close to zero
All Zener diodes have a positive temperature coefficient
Low-voltage (below 4 V) Zeners have a positive temperature coefficient
The temperature coefficient is independent of the breakdown voltage
questions.explanation: Field-emission breakdown (low voltage) has a negative coefficient and avalanche breakdown (high voltage) a positive one; around 5 to 6 V the two effects nearly cancel.

questions.questionText: A Zener regulator has V_in = 20 V, series resistor R_S = 200 Ω, V_Z = 10 V and a 1 kΩ load. The Zener current is:

A Zener regulator has V_in = 15 V, R_S = 100 Ω and V_Z = 9 V. The Zener needs at least 5 mA to stay in regulation. The smallest load resistance that can be connected while keeping regulation is about:
questions.explanation: I_R = (15 − 9)/100 = 60 mA; maximum load current = 60 − 5 = 55 mA; R_L(min) = 9 V / 55 mA ≈ 164 Ω.

questions.questionText: A Zener regulator has V_in = 24 V, R_S = 120 Ω and V_Z = 12 V. If the load is disconnected, the power dissipated in the Zener diode is:
questions.explanation: With no load all the series current flows in the Zener: I_Z = (24 − 12)/120 = 100 mA, so P_Z = 12 V × 0.1 A = 1.2 W.

questions.questionText: A 6 V Zener regulator is fed from 12 V and must supply a 20 mA load while keeping 10 mA in the Zener. The required series resistance is:
An unloaded Zener regulator has R_S = 95 Ω and a Zener with dynamic resistance r_z = 5 Ω operating in breakdown. If the input voltage rises by 1 V, the output voltage rises by about:
questions.explanation: For changes the Zener acts as r_z, so ΔV_out = ΔV_in × r_z/(R_S + r_z) = 1 × 5/100 = 50 mV.

questions.questionText: A 10 V Zener diode is used in a regulator with V_in = 8 V, R_S = 1 kΩ and R_L = 1 kΩ. The output voltage is:
questions.explanation: With the Zener removed the load would see 8 × 1k/(1k + 1k) = 4 V, which is below V_Z, so the Zener stays off and the output is simply 4 V.

questions.questionText: The capacitance of a varactor diode decreases as the reverse bias is increased because:
options: The depletion region narrows, reducing the plate area
The depletion region widens, increasing the effective plate separation
Minority carriers are stored in the junction
The junction breaks down and conducts
questions.explanation: The depletion layer is the dielectric between two conducting regions; more reverse voltage widens it, so C = εA/W falls.

questions.questionText: An abrupt-junction varactor has C ∝ 1/√V_R (built-in potential neglected). If its capacitance is 40 pF at a reverse voltage of 4 V, its capacitance at 16 V is:
The dark current of a photodiode is:
options: The forward current at the knee voltage
The current produced by the maximum rated illumination
The current that flows during reverse breakdown
The small reverse current that flows when no light falls on it
questions.explanation: In reverse bias a photodiode carries only the thermally generated reverse saturation current in darkness; light adds a photocurrent proportional to illumination.

questions.questionText: The colour of light emitted by an LED is determined mainly by:
options: The magnitude of the forward current
The band-gap energy of the semiconductor material
The colour of the plastic package
The value of the series resistor
questions.explanation: Photon energy is roughly equal to the band gap, so λ ≈ hc/E_g; GaAs gives infrared, GaAsP red to yellow and GaN blue.

questions.questionText: Which statement about special-purpose diodes is NOT correct?
options: A tunnel diode is lightly doped so that its depletion region is very wide
A Schottky diode uses a metal-semiconductor junction
A varactor is operated in reverse bias as a voltage-variable capacitor
An LED emits light when carriers recombine under forward bias
questions.explanation: A tunnel diode is very heavily doped, giving an extremely thin depletion region through which electrons tunnel and a negative-resistance region; the other statements are correct.

questions.questionText: Which junction capacitance dominates in a pn diode under forward bias?
questions.explanation: Under forward bias the stored minority charge near the junction changes with voltage, giving a diffusion capacitance proportional to current; the transition capacitance of the depletion layer dominates in reverse bias.
